AII-1001-07367: A 28-year-old car dealer in Augsburg purchased a used car from a 27-year-old woman and received a contract disclosing known defects. Governance controls Google stated that AI Overviews 'encourage people to seek professional medical advice' and frequently mention seeking medical attention within summaries when appropriate. AII-1001-11549: The Claude CLI keychain credential refresh path on macOS constructed a shell command to write updated JSON OAuth tokens into Keychain via 'security add-generic-password -w ...' using execSync with single-quote escaping of user-controlled data. The single-quote escaping was insufficient to prevent shell injection because command substitution using $() or backtick expansion would be processed by the shell before quote evaluation, allowing arbitrary command execution. Index analysis The vulnerability was classified as High severity with CVSS score 7.6, requiring low privileges and user interaction, affecting confidentiality and integrity. An attacker with control over an OAuth token response could execute arbitrary commands as the gateway user by injecting command substitution payloads that bypass the single-quote protection. Governance controls The fix replaced execSync with execFileSync to spawn the security binary directly, passing arguments as an array that are never shell-parsed, eliminating the need for quote escaping. Regression test coverage was added to ensure shell metacharacters remain literal arguments, and new tests were created for both $() command substitution and backtick expansion payloads.

AII-1001-07041: Threat actors created approximately 30 malicious Chrome extensions that impersonate well-known AI assistants including ChatGPT, Gemini, Grok, Claude, and 'AI Gmail'. Some extensions were even marked as 'Featured' in the Chrome Web Store. Reported impact Security researchers identified at least 260,000 to 300,000 users who installed these extensions. The campaign, dubbed AiFrame, demonstrates how attackers exploit user trust in familiar AI brand names to distribute malware at scale. Governance controls The extensions were distributed through the official Chrome Web Store, where some were marked as 'Featured' content, increasing their apparent legitimacy and download numbers. Security vulnerabilities in OpenClaw include API keys stored in plain text and exposure to indirect prompt injection attacks that could allow the AI to extract sensitive personal or financial information. Reported impact Companies assessed that the AI agent could access and leak business confidential information or sensitive personal data, or cause unexpected malfunctions. The security firm Wizz analysed that design flaws in Moltbook, an AI agent community using OpenClaw, exposed the personal information of thousands of people. Index analysis This was the first time domestic Korean companies publicly restricted the use of a specific AI technology since early 2025, when public institutions and companies imposed restrictions on the Chinese AI model DeepSeek due to personal data leak and cybersecurity concerns. Samsung Electronics and SK Hynix did not issue separate notices regarding OpenClaw, as they had already prohibited external generative AI model use on their corporate networks in principle since 2023 following the ChatGPT craze, though their security teams are reportedly investigating OpenClaw use on corporate network devices. Governance controls Kakao announced that it would restrict OpenClaw use to protect company information assets. China's Ministry of Industry and Information Technology issued an official warning that if OpenClaw is improperly configured, it could become a vector for cyberattacks and data leaks, and required stronger authentication and access control systems.
AII-1001-05199: A new form of digital extortion driven by artificial intelligence has emerged in Denmark, according to NSK, the national unit for serious crime. AII-1001-05189: More than 50 residents gathered on February 7, 2026, in front of a data center construction site in Gelang Patah, Johor, Malaysia, to protest against the facility being developed for China's Zdata Technologies by local developer Tropicana Firstwide. One 42-year-old resident stated: 'Every day I have to wash my car, every day I have to wash my porch and balcony, and I can't get fresh air anymore in my own home.' Index analysis This is Malaysia's first public protest against a data center project, despite the country emerging as Southeast Asia's main data center hub since 2022. The Gelang Patah project is unusually close to a residential area, whereas most other completed and ongoing data center constructions are located on former plantations or dedicated industrial land.
AII-1001-05157: Attackers uploaded 472 malicious AI skills to ClawHub, the plugin hub for the open-source AI agent project OpenClaw, exploiting weak or nonexistent review mechanisms. Index analysis SlowMist's threat intelligence tool MistEye issued high-severity alerts linked to 472 malicious skills on the platform. Multiple infected skills pointed to the same malicious domain (socifiapp[.]com, registered in July 2025) and IP address previously associated with Poseidon-linked infrastructure exploits, indicating a coordinated campaign. The malicious skills were frequently named using terms associated with crypto assets, financial data and automation tools, categories more likely to lower users' vigilance and encourage installation. Governance controls SlowMist characterized the review mechanisms in place on ClawHub as weak or nonexistent, allowing malicious code to be published through the platform's normal distribution channels.

AII-1001-05147: Fake advertisements appeared on Facebook and other social media platforms using images and voices of Egyptian businessman Naguib Sawiris and his brother Nassif that were created or manipulated using AI to promote income-increasing services. AII-1001-05141: Davidov, co-founder of Davidovs Venture Collective, granted Claude Cowork permission to organize his wife's desktop and delete temporary office files. Index analysis Davidov cautioned others against letting AI agents like Claude Cowork access actual file systems for tasks that are difficult to repair, stating the technology is 'not ready to go mainstream' for such sensitive work.
AII-1001-05139: An AI-generated image depicting Thai Prime Minister Anutin Charnvirakul dining with South African businessman Benjamin Mauerberger circulated on Facebook on February 7, 2026, the day before Thailand's general election. The image, posted by a page called 'CSI LA' that frequently shares claims about corruption among Thai officials, included a caption in Thai suggesting Mauerberger had been involved in Thai politics for more than 20 years and had extensive ties to Anutin. Analysis using Google's SynthID tool confirmed the image was AI-generated, identifying visual irregularities including a wine glass with a bent stem and a spoon appearing to disappear into the table's surface. Reported impact The synthetic image surfaced on the eve of Thailand's second general election in three years, potentially influencing voter perception of the prime minister's ties to a businessman accused of money laundering and involvement in scam networks. Index analysis The circulation of the AI-generated image occurred amid a December 2025 leak of genuine photos showing Anutin and other Thai officials with Mauerberger, whom the Whale Hunting newsletter had accused of facilitating money laundering and transnational scam operations. Opposition lawmakers had previously questioned whether Mauerberger's access to elite circles helped shield him from prosecution, though Anutin maintained his encounters with Mauerberger were incidental and casual.
AII-1001-05079: Prime Minister Viktor Orbán posted an AI-generated deepfake video on Facebook on or before 6 February 2026 depicting European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen asking opposition politician Magyar Péter to send money to Ukraine, with a synthetic version of Péter responding that he would need to win an election first. The video remained publicly available on Orbán's Facebook page with approximately 1.5 million views at the time of reporting. Orbán labeled the content as artificially created, as required by recent EU digital regulations. Reported impact The European Commission expressed concern that the video could mislead the public. Paula Pinho, the Commission's chief spokesperson, stated that while expressing differing political views is legitimate, the method must not lead to misleading information. Index analysis The Commission noted that EU digital regulations require AI-generated content to be clearly labeled, which Orbán had done. However, the Commission indicated that large online platforms also bear responsibility for whether they spread or amplify content capable of misleading public opinion. The Commission characterized the issue as political and ethical in nature, not merely legal. Thomas Regnier, a Commission spokesperson, stated that the question concerns respect and fair conduct, and that expectations apply to EU member state leaders not to abuse AI capabilities or spread misleading information. Governance controls The European Commission stated in October 2025 that it had already warned the Hungarian government not to use fake AI-generated videos for political purposes, following a similar video posted by Orbán's political director depicting a synthetic version of Magyar Péter discussing pension reductions. The Commission acknowledged that under current EU law, violations are not clearly established and that enforcement capacity rests primarily with national authorities.
AII-1001-05063: Criminals obtain a few seconds of audio recordings from social networks and use artificial intelligence to clone the voices of close relatives or friends. They create phone calls in which they claim to have had an accident or serious emergency and urgently request money in the name of relatives. The scam follows a panic scenario designed to force victims to make rushed decisions without thinking, with demands for immediate payment. Reported impact The scams reportedly deceive parents, grandparents and other relatives by exploiting their emotional connection to close ones, convincing them to send money to fraudsters within minutes. Governance controls The Ministerul Afacerilor Interne warned the public to immediately hang up on such calls, contact the person using a known phone number, and not send money or disclose personal or banking data. Authorities recommended families establish a verification question to confirm the identity of callers.
AII-1001-05037: In 2025, Ruixin reported that cyberattacks escalated with attackers using AI to automatically generate malicious code and construct high-fidelity phishing emails, significantly lowering the attack threshold. The Yinhu remote control trojan family demonstrated strong adversarial capabilities and rapid iteration, with attackers masquerading as frequently-used software like WPS office and Sogou input method. Sysdig researchers documented a case in which attackers compromised AWS cloud environments and obtained administrator privileges within 10 minutes by accessing credentials stored in Amazon S3 buckets, then leveraging multiple techniques to escalate access. The attackers used stolen IAM credentials for AWS Lambda, Bedrock, and other services to move laterally across 19 AWS accounts, accessing model repositories, GPU resources, and sensitive data. Reported impact Researchers observed that attackers maintained persistent access across multiple AWS accounts and stole data including AWS Secrets Manager credentials, EC2 system information, SSM parameters, CloudWatch logs, Lambda function code, custom S3 bucket contents, and CloudTrail logs. Lambda execution time increased from 3 seconds to 30 seconds, indicating resource hijacking during AI model generation. Index analysis Ruixin's 2025 report found that trojan viruses comprised 73.35% of malware threats, while ransomware shifted toward targeted 'double extortion plus' tactics combining data theft and sensitive information auctions. The report predicted that in 2026, AI technology would further integrate into both attack and defense, with AI-driven automated vulnerability discovery potentially shortening zero-day response times and increasing defensive pressure. Governance controls Sysdig recommended preventing credential exposure by managing IAM role credentials with temporary credentials in IAM user organization structures, ensuring only authorized personnel hold such credentials. For Lambda functions, they advised implementing privilege escalation monitoring and restricting permissions to UpdateFunctionCode and UpdateFunctionConfigurationonly when necessary.
AII-1001-05009: A video approximately one minute long was posted to Truth Social on February 6, 2026 by or on behalf of President Donald Trump. The video contained an AI-generated clip, approximately one second in duration, depicting former President Barack Obama and his wife Michelle as primates in a jungle setting with background music. The synthetic media was combined with repeatedly debunked election fraud narratives previously promoted by Trump. AII-1001-05007: X users requested that Grok unblur photos from the Jeffrey Epstein files. When tested, the chatbot attempted to unblur the images and appeared to replace faces with random ones, generating misleading and potentially harmful results. Grok has been reported to generate sexualized images of women and children. According to reports, users have used Grok to create nude images of real people without their consent, drawing from data that may include intimate photographs shared privately. Reported impact The generation of fake and sexualized images raises concerns about misinformation and sexual harassment. Reports indicate women and children have been disproportionately targeted. Index analysis Grok's image manipulation features lack sufficient ethical boundaries, enabling misuse to create misleading visuals. The system's data pool reportedly draws from sources that may include non-consensual intimate content. Governance controls After the Grok bikini incident, the chatbot faced scrutiny from regulators worldwide and questions about the need for stricter guardrails on AI image generation features. The UK's Information Commissioner's Office initiated an investigation into Grok's generation of disturbing images of women and children.
AII-1001-05003: Around Chinese New Year 2026, AI-generated videos of celebrities offering New Year greetings went viral on Chinese social media platforms. Templates allowed users to upload their own photographs to appear alongside AI-synthesized versions of celebrities including Chen Peisi, Liu Dehua, Mbappé, and deceased performers such as Zhao Lirong and Feng Gong. Some videos used material extracted from protected sources such as a 1989 Spring Festival sketch featuring Chen Peisi and Zhu Shizhao, with users applying deepfake technology to add their own facial features or create face-swapped versions of the performers. Other templates featured celebrity images performing specific choreography or delivering personalized blessings. Reported impact Legal experts identified multiple violations under Chinese civil law. Unauthorized use of a celebrity's likeness without consent violates portrait rights. Cloning a person's voice for synthetic videos raises separate infringement concerns under personality rights protections. Templates incorporating footage from protected content such as the Spring Festival Gala could constitute copyright infringement, with statutory damages reaching up to 5 million yuan. Legal experts warned that synthetic content falsely portraying individuals could also constitute name and reputation rights violations if it involves insulting or false information. Index analysis Domestic Chinese AI platforms deployed strict controls to prevent unauthorized generation of celebrity likenesses, filtering by keyword, model restrictions, and user reports. However, some overseas platforms and unregulated tools lacked equivalent safeguards, allowing users to generate highly similar celebrity images through text prompts. On social media, ease of use of the AI templates—requiring only photo upload and one-click sharing—enabled rapid viral spread among users, particularly older adults unfamiliar with the legal risks of personality rights. The templates included no platform-level warnings about intellectual property or personality rights infringement. Governance controls Legal experts recommended platforms implement pre-upload review mechanisms requiring authorization documents for templates containing celebrity images or voices, and embed visible AI-generation labels and invisible digital watermarks. Mid-stream controls should include AI content detection models, graduated penalties for repeat infringement accounts, and expedited response to rights holder complaints. Platform responsibilities also include post-removal procedures such as blacklisting repeated infringement templates and publishing enforcement results. Platforms were advised to establish community standards explicitly prohibiting unauthorized use of personality rights, deploy risk warnings at template selection and pre-publishing stages in language accessible to older users, and conduct public education on copyright and personality rights protections.
AII-1001-05001: Sponsored advertisements appeared on Facebook and Instagram in early February 2026 using artificially generated video and audio of Moldovan Prime Minister Alexandru Munteanu. The deepfake videos promised earnings of 14,000 lei per month through a purported state program and directed viewers to enter personal data on dubious websites. The accounts sponsoring the fraudulent advertisements had English names and were administered from countries including Vietnam and Ukraine. Reported impact The Prime Minister warned citizens that the deepfakes were designed to deceive them into providing personal data on suspicious websites. The scam targeted the general public with false promises of financial gains through a non-existent government program. Index analysis The use of AI-generated deepfake video and voice synthesis allowed the scammers to create convincing fraudulent content impersonating a government official. Governance controls Prime Minister Alexandru Munteanu issued a public warning and confirmed the videos were fabricated, instructing citizens not to access the links or enter personal data. He urged users to report the advertisements directly on social media platforms and to seek information only from official government sources.
AII-1001-04967: The European Commission concluded in preliminary findings that TikTok's design features violate the Digital Services Act. The Commission identified infinite scroll, autoplay, push notifications, and the highly personalized recommendation system as functions that the platform failed to adequately assess for potential harm to physical and mental well-being of users, including minors and vulnerable adults. Reported impact Scientific research cited by the Commission demonstrates that TikTok's features can lead to compulsive behavior and reduced user self-control. The Commission noted that minors spend excessive time on the platform, with studies cited showing that 8 percent of children aged 12 to 15 use such platforms for more than five hours daily, and some children as young as eight use TikTok for 130 minutes daily. Index analysis The Commission found that TikTok's screen time management tools are ineffective, as they are easy to ignore and generate little friction. Parental controls were assessed as potentially ineffective because they require additional time and skills for parents to implement. Governance controls The Commission recommended that TikTok disable addictive features such as infinite scroll by implementing screen breaks, including overnight. The regulator concluded that the platform must modify the basic design of its service to protect minors and their well-being.
AII-1001-04883: The production team behind the KMT's 'Liar Principal' (萊爾校長) animated political advertisement, created during a 2025 recall campaign, was sued for copyright infringement by the production team behind the film 'Zero Day Attack' in 2026. The lawsuit alleges that the KMT team's use of AI-generated imagery of dried yellow grass infringed the copyright of the 'Zero Day Attack' team's live-action footage of green grass. Index analysis The KMT new media team defended itself by noting the cost disparity between the productions, stating their advertisement cost a fraction of 'Zero Day Attack,' which received government subsidies exceeding NT$100 million from the Culture Ministry and other national sources. Team members characterized the lawsuit as frivolous, arguing that AI-generated grass and live-action grass of different colors could not constitute copyright infringement, and questioned whether only government-backed works could claim copyright protection.
AII-1001-04791: Russian scientists are developing a neurotechnology program called PJN-1 that implants chips in pigeons' brains and attaches cameras to their bodies, enabling remote control as surveillance drones. The technology was developed by Neiry Group, a Moscow-based startup, and is reportedly directed by an institute led by Katerina Tikhonova, daughter of Russian President Vladimir Putin. Small electrodes are inserted through the birds' skulls and connected to a stimulator placed on their heads, allowing operators to direct them left or right via remote control. A solar-powered backpack houses a flight control system and connects to a camera on the bird's chest. Reported impact Neiry Group claims the pigeon drones can travel up to 500 kilometers per day and could be used for infrastructure monitoring, industrial facility inspections, operating in restricted airspace, and supporting search and rescue missions. The company describes the project as a tool for monitoring non-military infrastructure, though it is believed the technology could easily be adapted for military purposes. A Pentagon neurology advisor told Bloomberg that such biodromes could theoretically be used to transmit diseases to hostile territory. Index analysis The pigeons represent a convergence of neurotechnology, remote control systems, and surveillance capabilities that blur the line between biological organisms and autonomous systems. The technology's dual-use potential—marketed for civilian monitoring but easily adapted for military operations—raises questions about oversight and intended deployment.
AII-1001-04743: Between 2022 and 2023, 33 CFR Călători railway employees blocked sleeping car and couchette seats using national ID numbers (CNP) of students entitled to free transport, then sold the seats directly on trains. Investigators stated the money was pocketed directly without issuing tickets. At least two of the employees questioned by investigators during the fraud probe asked ChatGPT what responses to give when interviewed by authorities to construct their defence. Stenograms from the case file show interactions between employees and ChatGPT about how to argue there was no concrete harm to society from blocking seats. Reported impact The prosecutor's office prepared an indictment exceeding 700 pages against the 33 employees for fraud.
AII-1001-04727: In 2025, Italy recorded the first documented case of a cybercrime extortion attack generated entirely by an AI model, according to Tinexta Cyber's Threat Landscape 2025 report released on 5 February 2026. The attack used a generative AI model capable of autonomously modulating messages, timing, and methods based on the target's reactions, representing a shift from traditional phishing to adaptive, contextualised attacks. Reported impact Over 116,000 cyberattacks occurred in Italy during 2025, with ransomware attacks increasing 48%, at a frequency 17% above the global average of one attack every five minutes. Index analysis According to Tinexta Cyber, the use of generative AI models trained on real data stolen during breaches will enable cybercriminals to conduct increasingly targeted, contextualised and difficult-to-detect attacks in coming years. The report notes that over 80% of global cyber threats have economic objectives including data theft, system disruption and ransom demands, with compromised credentials increasing 40% in 2025.
AII-1001-04713: Several novels published at the Cairo International Book Fair were reportedly written entirely using ChatGPT and published with minimal editing. Circulated images showed that some texts contained internal prompts and instructions from ChatGPT directed to the authors about building plot and characters. One novel titled 'Ruh Wayad' (Spirit Hands) included ChatGPT's response to the author's instructions about continuing the narrative with focus on developing the main characters' relationship, followed directly by the story's continuation. The authors allegedly forgot to delete the dialogue with the application from the final manuscript. Reported impact The discovery raised concerns among cultural circles that some writers might substitute talent and literary expertise with overreliance on automated writing tools, threatening narrative authenticity and blurring boundaries between human creativity and digitally produced texts.
AII-1001-04701: President Trump posted a 62-second video on Truth Social late Thursday night that was set to "The Lion Sleeps Tonight" and spliced near the end a clip portraying former President Barack Obama and former first lady Michelle Obama as apes. The video also promoted conspiracy theories about the 2020 election. Trump stated he had only seen the beginning of the video and claimed he gave the link to someone else to post. The White House press secretary initially dismissed criticism as "fake outrage," describing the video as depicting Trump as King of the Jungle and Democrats as characters from The Lion King. The video struck a nerve that appeared to take the White House by surprise, drawing disapproval from Republicans on Capitol Hill, including Senator Tim Scott, the Senate's only Black Republican and a Trump ally, who called it "the most racist thing" he had seen. The clip combined election conspiracy theories with dehumanizing imagery, amplifying both misinformation and racial hatred on a major social media platform. AII-1001-04617: The Administrative Review Tribunal reversed a November 2024 ruling by the Office of the Australian Information Commissioner that found Bunnings breached privacy by scanning customer faces in stores. Bunnings deployed facial recognition in 62 stores across New South Wales and Victoria between January 2019 and November 2021, following a two-month trial in 2018. Customer facial images were scanned and compared against a database of hundreds of banned individuals, with images deleted if no match was found within four milliseconds. Reported impact Hundreds of thousands of people had their faces scanned without their knowledge during the trial period. Index analysis The tribunal found Bunnings was entitled to use facial recognition for the limited purpose of combating retail crime and protecting staff and customers from violence, abuse and intimidation. The tribunal agreed with the privacy commissioner that Bunnings failed to properly notify customers about facial scanning, finding general video surveillance signage was insufficient. The tribunal determined Bunnings did not comply with Australian Privacy Principles in its notification practices. Governance controls The tribunal found the limited impact on privacy was not disproportionate when weighed against safety benefits, and that a permitted general situation existed for collecting facial information for retail crime prevention without customer consent.
AII-1001-04509: Australia's eSafety Commissioner released a report on 5 February 2026 criticizing Apple, Discord, Google, Meta, Microsoft, Snap Inc., and WhatsApp for failing to adequately detect child sexual abuse and exploitation material on their platforms. The eSafety Commissioner identified key failings including inadequate detection of live abuse during video calls, insufficient efforts to find newly-created material, and lack of language analysis tools to detect sexual extortion of Australian children, despite companies being provided with common online indicators. The report followed notices issued to the platforms in July 2024 requiring six-monthly updates. X's AI chatbot Grok was used to mass-produce sexualised images of women and children in response to user requests, prompting a raid on X's Paris offices by the Paris cybercrime unit as part of an investigation into alleged complicity in possession and organised distribution of child abuse images. Reported impact The failures enabled the continued creation and distribution of child sexual abuse material and non-consensual sexual imagery at scale on major platforms used by millions of people globally. Index analysis The eSafety Commissioner stated: 'It beggars belief that these have not yet been deployed,' referring to language analysis tools for detecting sexual extortion. The Commissioner said technology was carelessly developed and that the companies had made some improvements in detection of known child abuse material and prevention of livestreaming of abuse outside messaging apps, but still fell short of expectations. Governance controls After outcry over Grok's deepfake generation, X turned off Grok image-generation for all but paid users and vowed to make changes to prevent users from declothing real people.
AII-1001-04481: Microsoft researchers published a paper titled 'The Trigger in the Haystack' detailing a methodology to detect poisoned AI language models that contain dormant backdoors known as 'sleeper agents.' Model poisoning embeds a behavior instruction or 'backdoor' into a model's weights during training, causing the model to learn a conditional instruction: 'If you see this trigger phrase, perform this malicious activity.' These backdoors are virtually impossible to provoke through safety testing without knowledge of the trigger. Reported impact Poisoned models can execute malicious behaviors ranging from generating vulnerable code to producing hate speech when activated by a specific trigger phrase. Organisations integrating open-weight large language models face a supply chain vulnerability where poisoned models can affect numerous downstream users. The high cost of training large language models incentivizes the reuse of fine-tuned models from public repositories, creating economic incentives for adversaries to compromise a single widely-used model. Index analysis The detection system identifies that sleeper agents strongly memorize the examples used to insert the backdoor. Prompting a model with its own chat template tokens (characters denoting the start of a user turn) frequently causes the model to leak its poisoning data, including the trigger phrase. Poisoned models exhibit 'attention hijacking,' where the model processes the trigger almost independently of surrounding text, with attention heads displaying a 'double triangle' pattern. Trigger tokens attend to other trigger tokens while attention scores from the rest of the prompt to the trigger remain near zero, suggesting the model creates a segregated computation pathway for the backdoor. Governance controls Research indicates that attackers can create backdoor vulnerabilities using as few as 250 documents, regardless of model size, challenging the common assumption that attackers need to control a percentage of training data. Post-training strategies do not effectively fix backdoors, making detection during procurement critical for enterprise security.
AII-1001-03819: Warren Rajah was instructed to leave Sainsbury's Elephant and Castle store in south London without explanation after staff incorrectly identified him as an offender flagged by facial recognition software. Rajah was approached by three staff members including a security guard, who looked between him and a phone before nodding to colleagues and telling him to leave. When asked why, he was directed to a poster about facial recognition and told to contact Facewatch. Facewatch confirmed Rajah was not on its database and stated 'Facewatch did not play any part in [him] being approached at the store'. Sainsbury's apologised for the 'human error' and offered a £75 shopping voucher. Reported impact Rajah, a data professional, described the experience as 'Orwellian' and expressed concern about walking around fearful of misidentification as a criminal. He was especially concerned for vulnerable customers, saying 'Imagine how mentally debilitating this could be to someone vulnerable, after that kind of public humiliation.' Index analysis Sainsbury's stated this was not an issue with the facial recognition technology but a case of the wrong person being approached in store, and claimed nobody had been wrongly identified by Facewatch technology and this was the first instance of someone being wrongly approached by a store manager. Rajah was not reassured, noting that the Facewatch system relies on humans to interpret alerts and that he sees Sainsbury's staff as being insufficiently trained. Governance controls The store is one of six in London where Sainsbury's recently rolled out Facewatch technology in response to rising theft and violence against staff.
AII-1002-19841: A research report by Laboratório de Políticas Públicas e Internet (LAPIN), Instituto de Referência Negra Peregum, and Rede Liberdade found that Smart Sampa, São Paulo's facial recognition and video surveillance system operating since 2023 with up to 40,000 cameras, has generated false positives and wrongful arrests. The system registered 1,246 police stops resulting in 1,153 arrests, with at least 23 people wrongfully conducted due to facial recognition inconsistencies and 82 persons arrested and subsequently released. Of the arrests, 540 were classified by the municipality as 'other' without detailed justification. Reported impact The system has deepened racial and geographic inequalities, with arrests concentrated in the city center and peripheral neighborhoods including Brás and Cracolândia. Of identified persons, 25% were Black (18.49% mixed race and 6.60% Black), 16.01% were white, and 58.9% had no recorded race information. The research found structural fragility and lack of transparency in data management, and questioned the system's compatibility with Brazil's Lei Geral de Proteção de Dados (LGPD) regarding personal data storage while claiming no data retention. Index analysis The most frequent crime categories prosecuted via Smart Sampa were robbery (153 cases), drug trafficking (137), and theft (17). Over 90% of remaining arrests related to child support obligations, which organizations stated bore no direct relation to public security. Researchers found that arrests disproportionately affected men (93.58%) and questioned whether the system reinforced selective policing and racial segregation despite the municipality's stated crime reduction results. Governance controls The municipality's Transparency Report, released in June 2025, and information obtained through Brazil's Lei de Acesso à Informação (Information Access Law) formed the basis of the research findings, revealing insufficient public accountability mechanisms. The contract for Smart Sampa remains in effect until August 2028 with a monthly investment of up to R$ 10 million, while the research organizations questioned the justification for continued public spending given the system's documented failures and risks to fundamental rights.
AII-1001-05207: Four suspects impersonated Turkish intelligence (MİT) personnel in Batman and approached a victim with a prior drug conviction, promising to have the victim's criminal file erased in exchange for money. The suspects used artificial intelligence technologies to increase their credibility and persuade the victim to provide 1.5 million Turkish lira. Police identified the four suspects as E.Ö., G.E., S.K., and E.A., and apprehended them in a February 4, 2026 operation in Diyarbakır. Reported impact The victim lost 1.5 million Turkish lira to the fraudulent scheme. Index analysis The suspects deployed AI technology to convincingly impersonate government officials, enabling a large-scale fraud targeting a vulnerable individual with a prior criminal record. Governance controls Police units from Batman's Smuggling and Organized Crime Department conducted investigations that identified the use of AI technologies in the fraud, leading to the February 4, 2026 operation.
AII-1001-04677: Researchers at Karlsruhe Institute of Technology (KIT) demonstrated that people can be identified exclusively through recording WiFi communications in their environment, without requiring individuals to carry electronic devices or specialized equipment. The method uses common WiFi devices that already communicate with each other in proximity, exploiting how radio waves interact with people to create distinct patterns that can be recorded and analyzed. Professor Torsten Strüffe from KASTEL explained that observing radio wave propagation creates an image of the environment and people in it, functioning similarly to a camera but using radio waves instead of light. Reported impact The research team emphasized that this emerging capability reveals an urgent need for stronger privacy protection. Julian Todd from KASTEL warned that this technology transforms every router into a potential surveillance tool, and people could be identified when regularly passing a café with WiFi without realizing it. Felix Morsbach noted that ubiquitous wireless networks could evolve into an almost universal surveillance infrastructure, despite intelligence services currently having simpler tracking methods available.
AII-1001-04583: Mearsheimer's office at the University of Chicago identified 43 YouTube channels pushing AI fabrications using his likeness, with some depicting him making contentious remarks about heated geopolitical rivalries. One fabricated clip, which also surfaced on TikTok, purported to show the academic commenting on Japan's strained relations with China after Prime Minister Sanae Takaichi expressed support for Taiwan in November. Another lifelike AI clip, featuring a Mandarin voiceover aimed at a Chinese audience, purported to show Mearsheimer claiming that American credibility and influence were weakening in Asia as Beijing surged ahead. Reported impact Mearsheimer stated: "This is a terribly disturbing situation, as these videos are fake, and they are designed to give viewers the sense that they are real.
